stops.name: London, St Giles-without-Cripplegate
stops.campa: Outside London's wall, by the gate the lame have made their own, a church of Saint Giles stands from Norman days: St Giles-without-Cripplegate, the crippled patron at the cripples' gate, the plainest sentence the cult ever wrote. Fire and war will take the church again and again; the Blitz will gut it to the shell; and again and again it is raised, indestructible as the legend it serves. Milton will be buried in it. The beggars of every century know the door, and the door, in the manner of Giles's doors, is always there.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the crypt consecrated by Pope Urban II
stops.campa: Four centuries on, the tomb has become a nation of the road. Pope Urban II, fresh from preaching the Crusade at Clermont, comes in person to consecrate the altar of the great new abbey church rising over the hermit's cave. Saint-Gilles is now named the fourth pilgrimage of Christendom, after Jerusalem, after Rome, after Compostela, and the crypt where the abbot lies is a stone harbor for ten thousand crutches. The cripples come to the crippled saint, and the wounded hand, still open in eternity, receives them all.

stops.name: Oxford, St Giles' Church at the north gate of the town
stops.campa: At the edge of Oxford, where the town frays into fields, for Giles's churches keep to the margins, the gates, the places where travelers and the poor wash up, a church is consecrated in his name about the year 1120. The broad street before it takes his name too, and once a year erupts into St Giles' Fair around his September feast, the whole city trading and rejoicing on the hermit's doorstep, exactly the tumult he fled and exactly the abundance he fed to others. England will count over a hundred and fifty ancient churches under his name.

stops.name: Edinburgh, St Giles' Cathedral on the High Street
stops.campa: The name takes ship as the doors once did. In the days of King David I a church rises on the spine of Edinburgh's rock and is given to the hermit of Provence; it grows into the High Kirk of Scotland, and the Athenian who fled every city becomes the patron of a capital. His arm-bone, they say, comes north as a relic; his hind walks into the city's arms and seals. On the Royal Mile the beggars gather at Saint Giles' door as they gathered at the cave-mouth, and are in the right place.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the Romanesque facade and the Via Tolosana
stops.campa: The west front rises: three portals in the Roman manner, apostles ranked in carved stone, one of the glories of Romanesque Provence: the cypress doors of the legend answered at last in marble. Beneath it flows the Via Tolosana, the southernmost road of Saint James, and every pilgrim bound from Arles to Compostela passes through Saint-Gilles as through a needle's eye: they kneel at the hermit's tomb on the way to the apostle's. The abbey stands where the thicket stood, and the road itself is the hind's path, worn continental.

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, among the Fourteen Holy Helpers
stops.campa: In Franconia a shepherd boy sees the Christ Child ringed by fourteen children of light, who ask a chapel of him: the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and Giles stands among them: the only one of the fourteen who was not a martyr, admitted on the strength of a wound he refused to heal. Where plague and desperation press, his name is invoked against crippling, against terror, against the sin too shameful to confess. The basilica of Vierzehnheiligen will rise on the meadow of the vision, and in its glory of gold and stucco the hermit of the thicket keeps his place, still holding the arrow.
